   8  
   9  To install TinyDB from PyPI, run::

  12

  15

  17  
  18  
  19  Basic Usage
  20  -----------
  21  
  22  Let's cover the basics before going more into detail. We'll start by setting up
  23  a TinyDB database:
  24  
  25  >>> from tinydb import TinyDB, Query
  26  >>> db = TinyDB('db.json')
  27  
  28  You now have a TinyDB database that stores its data in ``db.json``.
  29  What about inserting some data? TinyDB expects the data to be Python ``dict``\s:
  30  
  31  >>> db.insert({'type': 'apple', 'count': 7})
  32  >>> db.insert({'type': 'peach', 'count': 3})
  33  
  34  .. note:: The ``insert`` method returns the inserted document's ID. Read more
  35            about it here: :ref:`document_ids`.
  36  
  37  
  38  Now you can get all documents stored in the database by running:
  39  
  40  >>> db.all()
  41  [{'count': 7, 'type': 'apple'}, {'count': 3, 'type': 'peach'}]
  42  
  43  You can also iter over stored documents:
  44  
  45  >>> for item in db:
  46  >>>     print(item)

  51

  55  >>> db.search(Fruit.count > 5)

  57

  60  
  61  >>> db.update({'count': 10}, Fruit.type == 'apple')

  64  
  65

  67  
  68  >>> db.remove(Fruit.count < 5)

  73  
  74  >>> db.truncate()

  79  Recap
  80  *****
  81  
  82  Before we dive deeper, let's recapitulate the basics:
  83  
  84  +-------------------------------+---------------------------------------------------------------+
  85  | **Inserting**                                                                                 |
  86  +-------------------------------+---------------------------------------------------------------+
  87  | ``db.insert(...)``            | Insert a document                                             |
  88  +-------------------------------+---------------------------------------------------------------+
  89  | **Getting data**                                                                              |
  90  +-------------------------------+---------------------------------------------------------------+
  91  | ``db.all()``                  | Get all documents                                             |
  92  +-------------------------------+---------------------------------------------------------------+
  93  | ``iter(db)``                  | Iter over all documents                                       |
  94  +-------------------------------+---------------------------------------------------------------+
  95  | ``db.search(query)``          | Get a list of documents matching the query                    |
  96  +-------------------------------+---------------------------------------------------------------+
  97  | **Updating**                                                                                  |
  98  +-------------------------------+---------------------------------------------------------------+
  99  | ``db.update(fields, query)``  | Update all documents matching the query to contain ``fields`` |
 100  +-------------------------------+---------------------------------------------------------------+
 101  | **Removing**                                                                                  |
 102  +-------------------------------+---------------------------------------------------------------+
 103  | ``db.remove(query)``          | Remove all documents matching the query                       |
 104  +-------------------------------+---------------------------------------------------------------+
 105  | ``db.truncate()``             | Remove all documents                                          |
 106  +-------------------------------+---------------------------------------------------------------+
 107  | **Querying**                                                                                  |
 108  +-------------------------------+---------------------------------------------------------------+
 109  | ``Query()``                   | Create a new query object                                     |
 110  +-------------------------------+---------------------------------------------------------------+
 111  | ``Query().field == 2``        | Match any document that has a key ``field`` with value        |
 112  |                               | ``== 2`` (also possible: ``!=``, ``>``, ``>=``, ``<``, ``<=``)|
 113  +-------------------------------+---------------------------------------------------------------+
 114  
 115  .. note::
 116  
 117      Query comparisons only support literal values on the right-hand side.
 118      Field-to-field comparisons like ``Query().a == Query().b`` are not
 119      supported. Use a callable predicate like
 120      ``db.search(lambda doc: doc.get('a') == doc.get('b'))`` for custom logic.
 121  
 122  .. note::
 123  
 124      Callables passed to query APIs (e.g. ``lambda`` predicates or ``Query().map``)
 125      execute in-process and must **never** be derived from untrusted or user-controlled
 126      input.

  40

  42  
  43          As an optimization, a query cache is implemented using a
  44          :class:`~tinydb.utils.LRUCache`. This class mimics the interface of
  45          a normal ``dict``, but starts to remove the least-recently used entries
  46          once a threshold is reached.

  49          data, the whole cache is discarded as the query results may have

  58          - ``document_id_class`` defines the class that is used to represent
  59            document IDs,
  60          - ``query_cache_class`` defines the class that is used for the query
  61            cache

  63            the query cache

  97          name: str,
  98          cache_size: int = default_query_cache_capacity,

 103          """

 106          self._name = name
 107          self._query_cache: LRUCache[QueryLike, list[Document]] \
 108              = self.query_cache_class(capacity=cache_size)

 110          self._next_id: Optional[int] = None

 112          # when reopen/construct with persist_empty=True (see issue #636).

  22  If that causes problems, you can write
  23  :doc:`your own storage <extend>`, that uses a more powerful (but also slower)
  24  library like `pickle <http://docs.python.org/library/pickle.html>`_ or
  25  `PyYAML <http://pyyaml.org/>`_.
  26  
  27  .. hint:: Opening multiple TinyDB instances on the same data (e.g. with the
  28     ``JSONStorage``) may result in unexpected behavior due to query caching.
  29     See query_caching_ on how to disable the query cache.
  30  
  31  Queries
  32  -------
  33  
  34  With that out of the way, let's start with TinyDB's rich set of queries.
  35  There are two main ways to construct queries. The first one resembles the
  36  syntax of popular ORM tools:
  37  
  38  >>> from tinydb import Query
  39  >>> User = Query()
  40  >>> db.search(User.name == 'John')
  41  
  42  As you can see, we first create a new Query object and then use it to specify
  43  which fields to check. Searching for nested fields is just as easy:
  44  
  45  >>> db.search(User.birthday.year == 1990)
  46  
  47  Not all fields can be accessed this way if the field name is not a valid Python
  48  identifier. In this case, you can switch to dict access notation:
  49  
  50  >>> # This would be invalid Python syntax:
  51  >>> db.search(User.country-code == 'foo')
  52  >>> # Use this instead:
  53  >>> db.search(User['country-code'] == 'foo')
  54  
  55  In addition, you can use arbitrary transform function where a field would be,
  56  for example:
  57  
  58  >>> from unidecode import unidecode
  59  >>> db.search(User.name.map(unidecode) == 'Jose')
  60  >>> # will match 'José' etc.
  61  
  62  The second, traditional way of constructing queries is as follows:
  63  
  64  >>> from tinydb import where
  65  >>> db.search(where('field') == 'value')
  66  
  67  Using ``where('field')`` is a shorthand for the following code:
  68  
  69  >>> db.search(Query()['field'] == 'value')
  70  
  71  Accessing nested fields with this syntax can be achieved like this:
  72  
  73  >>> db.search(where('birthday').year == 1900)
  74  >>> db.search(where('birthday')['year'] == 1900)
  75  
  76  Advanced queries
  77  ................
  78  
  79  In the :doc:`getting-started` you've learned about the basic comparisons
  80  (``==``, ``<``, ``>``, ...). In addition to these TinyDB supports the following
  81  queries:
  82  
  83  >>> # Existence of a field:
  84  >>> db.search(User.name.exists())
  85  
  86  >>> # Regex:
  87  >>> # Full item has to match the regex:
  88  >>> db.search(User.name.matches('[aZ]*'))
  89  >>> # Case insensitive search for 'John':
  90  >>> import re
  91  >>> db.search(User.name.matches('John', flags=re.IGNORECASE))
  92  >>> # Any part of the item has to match the regex:
  93  >>> db.search(User.name.search('b+'))
  94  
  95  >>> # Custom test:
  96  >>> test_func = lambda s: s == 'John'
  97  >>> db.search(User.name.test(test_func))
  98  
  99  >>> # Custom test with parameters:
 100  >>> def test_func(val, m, n):
 101  >>>     return m <= val <= n
 102  >>> db.search(User.age.test(test_func, 0, 21))
 103  >>> db.search(User.age.test(test_func, 21, 99))
 104  
 105  Another case is if you have a ``dict`` where you want to find all documents
 106  that match this ``dict``. We call this searching for a fragment:
 107  
 108  >>> db.search(Query().fragment({'foo': True, 'bar': False}))
 109  [{'foo': True, 'bar': False, 'foobar: 'yes!'}]
 110  
 111  You also can search for documents where a specific field matches the fragment:
 112  
 113  >>> db.search(Query().field.fragment({'foo': True, 'bar': False}))
 114  [{'field': {'foo': True, 'bar': False, 'foobar: 'yes!'}]
 115  
 116  When a field contains a list, you also can use the ``any`` and ``all`` methods.
 117  There are two ways to use them: with lists of values and with nested queries.
 118  Let's start with the first one. Assuming we have a user object with a groups list
 119  like this:
 120  
 121  >>> db.insert({'name': 'user1', 'groups': ['user']})
 122  >>> db.insert({'name': 'user2', 'groups': ['admin', 'user']})
 123  >>> db.insert({'name': 'user3', 'groups': ['sudo', 'user']})
 124  
 125  Now we can use the following queries:
 126  
 127  >>> # User's groups include at least one value from ['admin', 'sudo']
 128  >>> db.search(User.groups.any(['admin', 'sudo']))
 129  [{'name': 'user2', 'groups': ['admin', 'user']},
 130   {'name': 'user3', 'groups': ['sudo', 'user']}]
 131  >>>
 132  >>> # User's groups include all values from ['admin', 'user']
 133  >>> db.search(User.groups.all(['admin', 'user']))
 134  [{'name': 'user2', 'groups': ['admin', 'user']}]
 135  
 136  In some cases you may want to have more complex ``any``/``all`` queries.
 137  This is where nested queries come in as helpful. Let's set up a table like this:
 138  
 139  >>> Group = Query()
 140  >>> Permission = Query()
 141  >>> groups = db.table('groups')
 142  >>> groups.insert({
 143          'name': 'user',
 144          'permissions': [{'type': 'read'}]})
 145  >>> groups.insert({
 146          'name': 'sudo',
 147          'permissions': [{'type': 'read'}, {'type': 'sudo'}]})
 148  >>> groups.insert({
 149          'name': 'admin',
 150          'permissions': [{'type': 'read'}, {'type': 'write'}, {'type': 'sudo'}]})
 151  
 152  Now let's search this table using nested ``any``/``all`` queries:
 153  
 154  >>> # Group has a permission with type 'read'
 155  >>> groups.search(Group.permissions.any(Permission.type == 'read'))
 156  [{'name': 'user', 'permissions': [{'type': 'read'}]},
 157   {'name': 'sudo', 'permissions': [{'type': 'read'}, {'type': 'sudo'}]},
 158   {'name': 'admin', 'permissions':
 159          [{'type': 'read'}, {'type': 'write'}, {'type': 'sudo'}]}]
 160  >>> # Group has ONLY permission 'read'
 161  >>> groups.search(Group.permissions.all(Permission.type == 'read'))
 162  [{'name': 'user', 'permissions': [{'type': 'read'}]}]
 163  
 164  
 165  As you can see, ``any`` tests if there is *at least one* document matching
 166  the query while ``all`` ensures *all* documents match the query.
 167  
 168  The opposite operation, checking if a single item is contained in a list,
 169  is also possible using ``one_of``:
 170  
 171  >>> db.search(User.name.one_of(['jane', 'john']))
 172  
 173  Query modifiers
 174  ...............
 175  
 176  TinyDB also allows you to use logical operations to modify and combine
 177  queries:
 178  
 179  >>> # Negate a query:
 180  >>> db.search(~ (User.name == 'John'))
 181  
 182  >>> # Logical AND:
 183  >>> db.search((User.name == 'John') & (User.age <= 30))
 184  
 185  >>> # Logical OR:
 186  >>> db.search((User.name == 'John') | (User.name == 'Bob'))
 187

 189  
 190      When using ``&`` or ``|``, make sure you wrap the conditions on both sides

 192  
 193      Also, when using negation (``~``) you'll have to wrap the query you want

   6  Installing TinyDB
   7  -----------------
   8  
   9  To install TinyDB from PyPI, run::
  10  
  11      $ pip install tinydb
  12  
  13  You can also grab the latest development version from GitHub_. After downloading
  14  and unpacking it, you can install it using::
  15  
  16      $ pip install .
  17  
  18  
  19  Basic Usage
  20  -----------
  21  
  22  Let's cover the basics before going more into detail. We'll start by setting up
  23  a TinyDB database:
  24  
  25  >>> from tinydb import TinyDB, Query
  26  >>> db = TinyDB('db.json')
  27  
  28  You now have a TinyDB database that stores its data in ``db.json``.
  29  What about inserting some data? TinyDB expects the data to be Python ``dict``\s:
  30  
  31  >>> db.insert({'type': 'apple', 'count': 7})
  32  >>> db.insert({'type': 'peach', 'count': 3})
  33  
  34  .. note:: The ``insert`` method returns the inserted document's ID. Read more
  35            about it here: :ref:`document_ids`.
  36  
  37  
  38  Now you can get all documents stored in the database by running:
  39  
  40  >>> db.all()
  41  [{'count': 7, 'type': 'apple'}, {'count': 3, 'type': 'peach'}]
  42  
  43  You can also iter over stored documents:
  44  
  45  >>> for item in db:
  46  >>>     print(item)
  47  {'count': 7, 'type': 'apple'}
  48  {'count': 3, 'type': 'peach'}
  49  
  50  Of course you'll also want to search for specific documents. Let's try:
  51  
  52  >>> Fruit = Query()
  53  >>> db.search(Fruit.type == 'peach')
  54  [{'count': 3, 'type': 'peach'}]
  55  >>> db.search(Fruit.count > 5)
  56  [{'count': 7, 'type': 'apple'}]
  57  
  58  
  59  Next we'll update the ``count`` field of the apples:
  60  
  61  >>> db.update({'count': 10}, Fruit.type == 'apple')
  62  >>> db.all()
  63  [{'count': 10, 'type': 'apple'}, {'count': 3, 'type': 'peach'}]
  64  
  65  
  66  In the same manner you can also remove documents:
  67  
  68  >>> db.remove(Fruit.count < 5)
  69  >>> db.all()
  70  [{'count': 10, 'type': 'apple'}]
  71  
  72  And of course you can throw away all data to start with an empty database:
  73  
  74  >>> db.truncate()
  75  >>> db.all()
  76  []
  77  
  78

  83  
  84  +-------------------------------+---------------------------------------------------------------+
  85  | **Inserting**                                                                                 |
  86  +-------------------------------+---------------------------------------------------------------+
  87  | ``db.insert(...)``            | Insert a document                                             |
  88  +-------------------------------+---------------------------------------------------------------+
  89  | **Getting data**                                                                              |
  90  +-------------------------------+---------------------------------------------------------------+
  91  | ``db.all()``                  | Get all documents                                             |
  92  +-------------------------------+---------------------------------------------------------------+

  95  | ``db.search(query)``          | Get a list of documents matching the query                    |

  97  | **Updating**                                                                                  |

  99  | ``db.update(fields, query)``  | Update all documents matching the query to contain ``fields`` |
 100  +-------------------------------+---------------------------------------------------------------+
 101  | **Removing**                                                                                  |
 102  +-------------------------------+---------------------------------------------------------------+
 103  | ``db.remove(query)``          | Remove all documents matching the query                       |
 104  +-------------------------------+---------------------------------------------------------------+
 105  | ``db.truncate()``             | Remove all documents                                          |
 106  +-------------------------------+---------------------------------------------------------------+
 107  | **Querying**                                                                                  |
 108  +-------------------------------+---------------------------------------------------------------+
 109  | ``Query()``                   | Create a new query object                                     |
 110  +-------------------------------+---------------------------------------------------------------+
 111  | ``Query().field == 2``        | Match any document that has a key ``field`` with value        |
 112  |                               | ``== 2`` (also possible: ``!=``, ``>``, ``>=``, ``<``, ``<=``)|

 116

  16  Introduction
  17  ************
  18  
  19  TinyDB is a lightweight document oriented database optimized for your happiness :)
  20  It's written in pure Python and has no external dependencies. The target are
  21  small apps that would be blown away by a SQL-DB or an external database server.
  22  
  23  TinyDB is:
  24  
  25  - **tiny:** The current source code has 1800 lines of code (with about 40%
  26    documentation) and 1600 lines tests.
  27  
  28  - **document oriented:** Like MongoDB_, you can store any document
  29    (represented as ``dict``) in TinyDB.
  30  
  31  - **optimized for your happiness:** TinyDB is designed to be simple and
  32    fun to use by providing a simple and clean API.
  33  
  34  - **written in pure Python:** TinyDB neither needs an external server (as
  35    e.g. `PyMongo <https://pymongo.readthedocs.io/en/stable/>`_) nor any dependencies
  36    from PyPI.
  37  
  38  - **works on Python 3.8+ and PyPy3:** TinyDB works on all modern versions of Python
  39    and PyPy.
  40  
  41  - **powerfully extensible:** You can easily extend TinyDB by writing new
  42    storages or modify the behaviour of storages with Middlewares.
  43  
  44  - **100% test coverage:** No explanation needed.
  45  
  46  To dive straight into all the details, head over to the `TinyDB docs
  47  <https://tinydb.readthedocs.io/>`_. You can also discuss everything related
  48  to TinyDB like general development, extensions or showcase your TinyDB-based
  49  projects on the `discussion forum <http://forum.m-siemens.de/.>`_.

1  How to Extend TinyDB
   2  ====================
   3  
   4  There are three main ways to extend TinyDB and modify its behaviour:
   5  
   6  1. custom storages,
   7  2. custom middlewares,
   8  3. use hooks and overrides, and
   9  4. subclassing ``TinyDB`` and ``Table``.
  10  
  11  Let's look at them in this order.
  12  
  13  Write a Custom Storage
  14  ----------------------
  15  
  16  First, we have support for custom storages. By default TinyDB comes with an
  17  in-memory storage and a JSON file storage. But of course you can add your own.
  18  Let's look how you could add a `YAML <http://yaml.org/>`_ storage using
  19  `PyYAML <http://pyyaml.org/wiki/PyYAML>`_:
  20  
  21  .. code-block:: python
  22  
  23      import yaml
  24  
  25      class YAMLStorage(Storage):
  26          def __init__(self, filename):  # (1)
  27              self.filename = filename
  28  
  29          def read(self):
  30              with open(self.filename) as handle:
  31                  try:
  32                      data = yaml.safe_load(handle.read())  # (2)
  33                      return data
  34                  except yaml.YAMLError:
  35                      return None  # (3)
  36  
  37          def write(self, data):
  38              with open(self.filename, 'w+') as handle:
  39                  yaml.dump(data, handle)
  40  
  41          def close(self):  # (4)
  42              pass
  43  
  44  There are some things we should look closer at:
  45  
  46  1. The constructor will receive all arguments passed to TinyDB when creating
  47     the database instance (except ``storage`` which TinyDB itself consumes).
  48     In other words calling ``TinyDB('something', storage=YAMLStorage)`` will
  49     pass ``'something'`` as an argument to ``YAMLStorage``.
  50     If you accept callables or other executable values in your storage
  51     constructor (or elsewhere), do not derive them from untrusted or
  52     user-controlled input.
  53  2. We use ``yaml.safe_load`` as recommended by the
  54     `PyYAML documentation <http://pyyaml.org/wiki/PyYAMLDocumentation#LoadingYAML>`_
  55     when processing data from a potentially untrusted source.
  56  3. If the storage is uninitialized, TinyDB expects the storage to return
  57     ``None`` so it can do any internal initialization that is necessary.
  58  4. If your storage needs any cleanup (like closing file handles) before an
  59     instance is destroyed, you can put it in the ``close()`` method. To run
  60     these, you'll either have to run ``db.close()`` on your ``TinyDB`` instance
  61     or use it as a context manager, like this:
  62  
  63     .. code-block:: python
  64  
  65          with TinyDB('db.yml', storage=YAMLStorage) as db:
  66              # ...
  67  
  68  Finally, using the YAML storage is very straight-forward:
  69  
  70  .. code-block:: python
  71  
  72      db = TinyDB('db.yml', storage=YAMLStorage)
  73      # ...
  74  
  75  
  76  Write Custom Middleware
  77  -------------------------
  78  
  79  Sometimes you don't want to write a new storage module but rather modify the
  80  behaviour of an existing one. As an example we'll build middleware that filters
  81  out empty items.
  82  
  83  Because middleware acts as a wrapper around a storage, they needs a ``read()``
  84  and a ``write(data)`` method. In addition, they can access the underlying storage
  85  via ``self.storage``. Before we start implementing we should look at the structure
  86  of the data that the middleware receives. Here's what the data that goes through
  87  the middleware looks like:
  88  
  89  .. code-block:: python
  90  
  91      {
  92          '_default': {
  93              1: {'key': 'value'},
  94              2: {'key': 'value'},
  95              # other items
  96          },
  97          # other tables
  98      }
  99  
 100  Thus, we'll need two nested loops:
 101  
 102  1. Process every table
 103  2. Process every item
 104  
 105  Now let's implement that:
 106  
 107  .. code-block:: python
 108  
 109      class RemoveEmptyItemsMiddleware(Middleware):
 110          def __init__(self, storage_cls):
 111              # Any middleware *has* to call the super constructor
 112              # with storage_cls
 113              super().__init__(storage_cls)  # (1)
 114  
 115          def read(self):
 116              data = self.storage.read()
 117  
 118              for table_name in data:
 119                  table_data = data[table_name]
 120  
 121                  for doc_id in table_data:
 122                      item = table_data[doc_id]
 123  
 124                      if item == {}:
 125                          del table_data[doc_id]
 126  
 127              return data
 128  
 129          def write(self, data):
 130              for table_name in data:
 131                  table_data = data[table_name]
 132  
 133                  for doc_id in table_data:
 134                      item = table_data[doc_id]
 135  
 136                      if item == {}:
 137                          del table_data[doc_id]
 138  
 139              self.storage.write(data)
 140  
 141          def close(self):
 142              self.storage.close()
 143  
 144  
 145  Note that the constructor calls the middleware constructor (1) and passes
 146  the storage class to the middleware constructor.
 147  
 148  To wrap storage with this new middleware, we use it like this:
 149  
 150  .. code-block:: python
 151  
 152      db = TinyDB(storage=RemoveEmptyItemsMiddleware(SomeStorageClass))

  16  Introduction

  18  
  19  TinyDB is a lightweight document oriented database optimized for your happiness :)
  20  It's written in pure Python and has no external dependencies. The target are
  21  small apps that would be blown away by a SQL-DB or an external database server.
  22  
  23  TinyDB is:
  24  
  25  - **tiny:** The current source code has 1800 lines of code (with about 40%
  26    documentation) and 1600 lines tests.
  27  
  28  - **document oriented:** Like MongoDB_, you can store any document

  31  - **optimized for your happiness:** TinyDB is designed to be simple and
  32    fun to use by providing a simple and clean API.

  35    e.g. `PyMongo <https://pymongo.readthedocs.io/en/stable/>`_) nor any dependencies

  42    storages or modify the behaviour of storages with Middlewares.

  44  - **100% test coverage:** No explanation needed.

  46  To dive straight into all the details, head over to the `TinyDB docs

   3  Getting Started
   4  ===============
   5  
   6  Installing TinyDB
   7  -----------------
   8  
   9  To install TinyDB from PyPI, run::
  10  
  11      $ pip install tinydb
  12  
  13  You can also grab the latest development version from GitHub_. After downloading
  14  and unpacking it, you can install it using::
  15  
  16      $ pip install .
  17  
  18  
  19  Basic Usage
  20  -----------
  21  
  22  Let's cover the basics before going more into detail. We'll start by setting up
  23  a TinyDB database:
  24  
  25  >>> from tinydb import TinyDB, Query
  26  >>> db = TinyDB('db.json')
  27  
  28  You now have a TinyDB database that stores its data in ``db.json``.
  29  What about inserting some data? TinyDB expects the data to be Python ``dict``\s:
  30  
  31  >>> db.insert({'type': 'apple', 'count': 7})
  32  >>> db.insert({'type': 'peach', 'count': 3})
  33  
  34  .. note:: The ``insert`` method returns the inserted document's ID. Read more
  35            about it here: :ref:`document_ids`.
  36  
  37  
  38  Now you can get all documents stored in the database by running:
  39  
  40  >>> db.all()
  41  [{'count': 7, 'type': 'apple'}, {'count': 3, 'type': 'peach'}]
  42  
  43  You can also iter over stored documents:
  44  
  45  >>> for item in db:
  46  >>>     print(item)
  47  {'count': 7, 'type': 'apple'}
  48  {'count': 3, 'type': 'peach'}
  49  
  50  Of course you'll also want to search for specific documents. Let's try:
  51  
  52  >>> Fruit = Query()
  53  >>> db.search(Fruit.type == 'peach')
  54  [{'count': 3, 'type': 'peach'}]
  55  >>> db.search(Fruit.count > 5)
  56  [{'count': 7, 'type': 'apple'}]
  57  
  58  
  59  Next we'll update the ``count`` field of the apples:
  60  
  61  >>> db.update({'count': 10}, Fruit.type == 'apple')
  62  >>> db.all()
  63  [{'count': 10, 'type': 'apple'}, {'count': 3, 'type': 'peach'}]
  64  
  65  
  66  In the same manner you can also remove documents:
  67  
  68  >>> db.remove(Fruit.count < 5)
  69  >>> db.all()
  70  [{'count': 10, 'type': 'apple'}]
  71  
  72  And of course you can throw away all data to start with an empty database:
  73  
  74  >>> db.truncate()
  75  >>> db.all()
  76  []
  77  
  78  
  79  Recap
  80  *****
  81  
  82  Before we dive deeper, let's recapitulate the basics:
  83  
  84  +-------------------------------+---------------------------------------------------------------+
  85  | **Inserting**                                                                                 |
  86  +-------------------------------+---------------------------------------------------------------+
  87  | ``db.insert(...)``            | Insert a document                                             |
  88  +-------------------------------+---------------------------------------------------------------+
  89  | **Getting data**                                                                              |
  90  +-------------------------------+---------------------------------------------------------------+
  91  | ``db.all()``                  | Get all documents                                             |
  92  +-------------------------------+---------------------------------------------------------------+
  93  | ``iter(db)``                  | Iter over all documents                                       |
  94  +-------------------------------+---------------------------------------------------------------+
  95  | ``db.search(query)``          | Get a list of documents matching the query                    |
  96  +-------------------------------+---------------------------------------------------------------+
  97  | **Updating**                                                                                  |
  98  +-------------------------------+---------------------------------------------------------------+
  99  | ``db.update(fields, query)``  | Update all documents matching the query to contain ``fields`` |
 100  +-------------------------------+---------------------------------------------------------------+
 101  | **Removing**                                                                                  |
 102  +-------------------------------+---------------------------------------------------------------+
 103  | ``db.remove(query)``          | Remove all documents matching the query                       |
 104  +-------------------------------+---------------------------------------------------------------+
 105  | ``db.truncate()``             | Remove all documents                                          |
 106  +-------------------------------+---------------------------------------------------------------+
 107  | **Querying**                                                                                  |
 108  +-------------------------------+---------------------------------------------------------------+
 109  | ``Query()``                   | Create a new query object                                     |
 110  +-------------------------------+---------------------------------------------------------------+
 111  | ``Query().field == 2``        | Match any document that has a key ``field`` with value        |
 112  |                               | ``== 2`` (also possible: ``!=``, ``>``, ``>=``, ``<``, ``<=``)|
 113  +-------------------------------+---------------------------------------------------------------+
 114  
 115  .. note::
 116  
 117      Query comparisons only support literal values on the right-hand side.
 118      Field-to-field comparisons like ``Query().a == Query().b`` are not
 119      supported. Use a callable predicate like
 120      ``db.search(lambda doc: doc.get('a') == doc.get('b'))`` for custom logic.
 121  
 122  .. note::
 123  
 124      Callables passed to query APIs (e.g. ``lambda`` predicates or ``Query().map``)
 125      execute in-process and must **never** be derived from untrusted or user-controlled
 126      input.

 129  .. _GitHub: http://github.com/msiemens/tinydb/

   6  Advanced Usage
   7  ==============
   8  
   9  Remarks on Storage
  10  ------------------
  11  
  12  Before we dive deeper into the usage of TinyDB, we should stop for a moment
  13  and discuss how TinyDB stores data.
  14  
  15  To convert your data to a format that is writable to disk TinyDB uses the
  16  `Python JSON <http://docs.python.org/2/library/json.html>`_ module by default.
  17  It's great when only simple data types are involved but it cannot handle more
  18  complex data types like custom classes. On Python 2 it also converts strings to
  19  Unicode strings upon reading
  20  (described `here <http://stackoverflow.com/q/956867/997063>`_).
  21  
  22  If that causes problems, you can write
  23  :doc:`your own storage <extend>`, that uses a more powerful (but also slower)
  24  library like `pickle <http://docs.python.org/library/pickle.html>`_ or
  25  `PyYAML <http://pyyaml.org/>`_.
  26  
  27  .. hint:: Opening multiple TinyDB instances on the same data (e.g. with the
  28     ``JSONStorage``) may result in unexpected behavior due to query caching.
  29     See query_caching_ on how to disable the query cache.
  30  
  31  Queries
  32  -------
  33  
  34  With that out of the way, let's start with TinyDB's rich set of queries.
  35  There are two main ways to construct queries. The first one resembles the
  36  syntax of popular ORM tools:
  37  
  38  >>> from tinydb import Query
  39  >>> User = Query()
  40  >>> db.search(User.name == 'John')
  41  
  42  As you can see, we first create a new Query object and then use it to specify
  43  which fields to check. Searching for nested fields is just as easy:
  44  
  45  >>> db.search(User.birthday.year == 1990)
  46  
  47  Not all fields can be accessed this way if the field name is not a valid Python
  48  identifier. In this case, you can switch to dict access notation:
  49  
  50  >>> # This would be invalid Python syntax:
  51  >>> db.search(User.country-code == 'foo')
  52  >>> # Use this instead:
  53  >>> db.search(User['country-code'] == 'foo')
  54  
  55  In addition, you can use arbitrary transform function where a field would be,
  56  for example:
  57  
  58  >>> from unidecode import unidecode
  59  >>> db.search(User.name.map(unidecode) == 'Jose')
  60  >>> # will match 'José' etc.
  61  
  62  The second, traditional way of constructing queries is as follows:
  63  
  64  >>> from tinydb import where
  65  >>> db.search(where('field') == 'value')
  66  
  67  Using ``where('field')`` is a shorthand for the following code:
  68  
  69  >>> db.search(Query()['field'] == 'value')
  70  
  71  Accessing nested fields with this syntax can be achieved like this:
  72  
  73  >>> db.search(where('birthday').year == 1900)
  74  >>> db.search(where('birthday')['year'] == 1900)
  75  
  76  Advanced queries
  77  ................
  78  
  79  In the :doc:`getting-started` you've learned about the basic comparisons
  80  (``==``, ``<``, ``>``, ...). In addition to these TinyDB supports the following
  81  queries:
  82  
  83  >>> # Existence of a field:
  84  >>> db.search(User.name.exists())
  85  
  86  >>> # Regex:
  87  >>> # Full item has to match the regex:
  88  >>> db.search(User.name.matches('[aZ]*'))
  89  >>> # Case insensitive search for 'John':
  90  >>> import re
  91  >>> db.search(User.name.matches('John', flags=re.IGNORECASE))
  92  >>> # Any part of the item has to match the regex:
  93  >>> db.search(User.name.search('b+'))
  94  
  95  >>> # Custom test:
  96  >>> test_func = lambda s: s == 'John'
  97  >>> db.search(User.name.test(test_func))
  98  
  99  >>> # Custom test with parameters:
 100  >>> def test_func(val, m, n):
 101  >>>     return m <= val <= n
 102  >>> db.search(User.age.test(test_func, 0, 21))
 103  >>> db.search(User.age.test(test_func, 21, 99))
 104  
 105  Another case is if you have a ``dict`` where you want to find all documents
 106  that match this ``dict``. We call this searching for a fragment:
 107  
 108  >>> db.search(Query().fragment({'foo': True, 'bar': False}))
 109  [{'foo': True, 'bar': False, 'foobar: 'yes!'}]
 110  
 111  You also can search for documents where a specific field matches the fragment:
 112  
 113  >>> db.search(Query().field.fragment({'foo': True, 'bar': False}))
 114  [{'field': {'foo': True, 'bar': False, 'foobar: 'yes!'}]
 115  
 116  When a field contains a list, you also can use the ``any`` and ``all`` methods.
 117  There are two ways to use them: with lists of values and with nested queries.
 118  Let's start with the first one. Assuming we have a user object with a groups list
 119  like this:
 120  
 121  >>> db.insert({'name': 'user1', 'groups': ['user']})
 122  >>> db.insert({'name': 'user2', 'groups': ['admin', 'user']})
 123  >>> db.insert({'name': 'user3', 'groups': ['sudo', 'user']})
 124  
 125  Now we can use the following queries:
 126  
 127  >>> # User's groups include at least one value from ['admin', 'sudo']
 128  >>> db.search(User.groups.any(['admin', 'sudo']))
 129  [{'name': 'user2', 'groups': ['admin', 'user']},
 130   {'name': 'user3', 'groups': ['sudo', 'user']}]
 131  >>>
 132  >>> # User's groups include all values from ['admin', 'user']
 133  >>> db.search(User.groups.all(['admin', 'user']))
 134  [{'name': 'user2', 'groups': ['admin', 'user']}]
 135  
 136  In some cases you may want to have more complex ``any``/``all`` queries.
 137  This is where nested queries come in as helpful. Let's set up a table like this:
 138  
 139  >>> Group = Query()
 140  >>> Permission = Query()
 141  >>> groups = db.table('groups')
 142  >>> groups.insert({
 143          'name': 'user',
 144          'permissions': [{'type': 'read'}]})
 145  >>> groups.insert({
 146          'name': 'sudo',
 147          'permissions': [{'type': 'read'}, {'type': 'sudo'}]})
 148  >>> groups.insert({
 149          'name': 'admin',
 150          'permissions': [{'type': 'read'}, {'type': 'write'}, {'type': 'sudo'}]})
 151  
 152  Now let's search this table using nested ``any``/``all`` queries:
 153  
 154  >>> # Group has a permission with type 'read'
 155  >>> groups.search(Group.permissions.any(Permission.type == 'read'))
 156  [{'name': 'user', 'permissions': [{'type': 'read'}]},
 157   {'name': 'sudo', 'permissions': [{'type': 'read'}, {'type': 'sudo'}]},
 158   {'name': 'admin', 'permissions':
 159          [{'type': 'read'}, {'type': 'write'}, {'type': 'sudo'}]}]
 160  >>> # Group has ONLY permission 'read'
 161  >>> groups.search(Group.permissions.all(Permission.type == 'read'))
 162  [{'name': 'user', 'permissions': [{'type': 'read'}]}]
